note: Original preparation paths. Refresher selections are editorial choices, not equivalence to the external courses. Advanced preparation paths link to available course modules; course coverage states the current scope.

paths.title: Foundations
paths.why: Start with the numbers and simple rules used in the first physics lessons.

steps.why: Read a fraction such as ¾ as three of four equal parts.
Read decimals such as 0.5, halfway between zero and one.
Use a minus sign for values below zero, such as −3 °C.
Use brackets to show which part of a calculation comes first.
Write repeated multiplication.
Put a known value into a rule.

paths.title: Mathematical toolkit
paths.why: Build the number skills used by the mathematical toolkit. Take as many small steps as you need.

steps.why: Read a fraction such as ¾ as three of four equal parts.
Read decimals such as 0.5, halfway between zero and one.
Use a minus sign for values below zero, such as −3 °C.
Read a percentage as a share of 100.
Use brackets to show which part of a calculation comes first.
Write repeated multiplication.
Find a square root. For example, 3 is the square root of 9 because 3 × 3 = 9.
Find one divided by a number.
Put a known value into a rule.
Use a rule to turn an input number into an output number.
See how one amount changes when you double the other.
Follow repeated growth.
Find the power that gives a number.
Use a small label below a letter to tell two readings apart.
Read the sum sign as an instruction to add a list of numbers.
Subtract the starting value from the final value.
Keep a measurement and its unit together.
Read how two quantities are connected.
Read change from a graph.
Find an unknown while keeping both sides equal.

Find the change between two readings.
Find the unknown in an equation.
Split a direction into components.

paths.title: Electricity & magnetism
paths.why: Review forces and fields before studying electric and magnetic effects.

steps.why: Keep charge, force and energy units clear.
Track the direction of a force.

Represent two linked number parts.

paths.why: Review energy, change and chance before studying heat.

Read logarithms used later in entropy.
Describe a small change.

Change one variable while holding another fixed.

Use a conservation rule.

paths.title: Light & optics
paths.why: Follow a wave crest, compare directions, and see what happens where two waves meet.

Compare angles.

Find the part that passes a polarizer.

Connect light with electric and magnetic waves.

paths.title: Relativity

steps.why: Keep units consistent.
State which assumptions you use.

paths.title: Atomic & nuclear physics
paths.why: Review quantum states, electric interactions and energy before studying atoms and nuclei.

steps.why: Read small and large scales.
Read a falling population.
Use chances and averages.

Track electric potential energy per charge.
Read the allowed energies of hydrogen.

Combine two spin states.
Place identical particles in allowed states.
Separate rest energy and motion energy.

paths.title: Particle physics

paths.why: Review waves, quantum states and temperature before studying matter in large groups.

paths.title: Astrophysics
paths.why: Review the tools used to learn about distant objects from motion and light.

steps.why: Read a number with real and imaginary parts.

paths.title: Advanced analytical mechanics
paths.why: Start with a position and an energy. These tools will help you compare different paths an object could take.

paths.title: Fluid dynamics
paths.why: Prepare to study flowing liquids and gases beyond the simple fluid lessons.

steps.why: Compare mass per volume.
Review pressure in a still fluid.
Track the upward pressure force.

Use energy within the ideal-flow limits.

Check whether more flow leaves a tiny region than enters it.

remainingTools: Partial differential equations: follow a quantity changing in space and time.

remainingTools: Partial differential equations: connect changes in space and time.

paths.title: General relativity
paths.why: Review how observers use clocks and rulers. You will use those tools to study gravity and free fall.

steps.why: Track change along different coordinates.
Read linear transformations.
Follow a changing path.
Locate events for an observer.
Compare spacetime separation.
Combine space and time components.
Connect a local gravity picture and acceleration.

Recognize where the introductory picture ends.

remainingTools: Tensor calculus: track quantities as coordinates change.
Differential geometry: measure distances and curvature.
Learn how to compare paths using action, calculate a response to a small source, and work out motion in many small time steps.
nextTopics: Use a metric to measure spacetime separation.
Compare directions at nearby points.
Describe curvature with tensors.

paths.title: Advanced experimental methods
